messages.subject: replacing clusters with individuals
messages.body_plain:
Hello distance samplers,

I have collected point transect data using clusters as the recording =
unit and want to correct for size bias.  The "Introduction to Distance =
Sampling" book (pg 167) states that one method is to replace clusters =
with individuals but then the assumption that detections are independent =
is violated.  I beleive I understand how to conduct the solution - =
analyze the clustered data then refit the same model to the individual =
data.  But, I don't understand how this solves the problem of =
independence of detections.

If anyone can provide information on how this method solves the problem =
of independence of detections I would greatly appreciate it.  I do not =
yet have a copy of the "Advanced Guide to DS" and a search of the email =
archive did not come up with anything.  Also, is there is any thought =
that stratification by cluster size would be a better approach?

Thanks in advance,
Scott

messages.subject: Re: replacing clusters with individuals
messages.body_plain:
Scott, this is a pragmatic solution.  Variance estimation methods in
Distance are remarkably robust to non-independence.  In fact, if you use
the bootstrap option based on lines or points, you don't assume that
detections are independent at all.  So there is nor real problem for
variance estimation.  But the following aspects of Distance are NOT
robust to non-independence:  goodness-of-fit (including
Kolmogorov-Smirnov and Cramer-von Mises) and AIC.  Hence there is a
tendency to select models with too many parameters.  To avoid this, you
can conduct model selection on the analysis of groups, where independent
detections is a more reasonable assumption.  You can then fit the
selected model to an analysis of individuals.

Personally, I don't think this is the best solution to your problem
though.  If you have data as clusters, why not just do the default
analysis, where you analyse clusters, and separately estimate mean
cluster size?  The default regression methods for this in Distance
corrects for size bias.  You could also consider using the MCDS engine,
with cluster size as a covariate.  There are limitations on what is
currently implemented in Distance in this case, e.g. if you have strata,
but it may do what you need.

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: Overestimation of density
messages.body_plain:
I am currently using the Distance software to fit my point count data to
estimate several songbird densities and have some concerns regarding my
chestnut-backed chickadee density estimate. The density estimate I obtain
using the best model is 4.5 birds/ha which is close to being 5x larger than
the density estimates for other birds I detected as well as much larger than
densities of chickadees from another study in the same national park.  I'm
afraid that I am grossly overestimating their densities and I am hoping to
find a way to fix this problem.
I've already right truncated the largest 5% of the distance detections and
I've read that left-truncating would only worsen the problem.  When looking
at the frequencies of distances, I do notice that there is no shoulder and
that my highest number of detections occur at 20m, thus suggesting evasive
movement, but I've read  evasive movement would cause underestimation of
density and not overestimation.

Has anyone experienced this or have suggestions for dealing with this issue?

Thanks,
Carly Gelarden
MS Candidate
Environmental Science
Western Washington University
CarlyGel...@msn.com

messages.subject: Re: Overestimation of density
messages.body_plain:
Carly,

 The first question that came to my mind is what is the reason
 for getting density estimates 5x larger than other species.
 Is it because you saw 5x more birds of this species or
 because you estimate a very low detection probability?

 If you saw 5x more birds (i.e., raw counts were much greater)
 then it may not be how you are estimating the detection fct
 but that you simply detected more birds.  If your raw counts
 are similar then the issue is with your detection function.

 You don't provide enough information in your email to assess
 what might be the problem with your det fct estimation.  For
 example,what proportion of birds are you estimating you
 detected, and what model are you fitting?  If you used a neg
 exponential fct it might the cause of your problems.

 Regards,

 Duane Diefenbach

messages.subject: Re: Overestimation of density
messages.body_plain:
Adding to Duane's comments, the hazard-rate model can also fit very
spiked, implausible detection functions.  For point transect data, you
often need to truncate more than 5% of the data - we suggest 10% in the
2001 book, but any cookbook rule is going to go wrong for many data
sets.  Again for point transect data, your highest frequency of
detections SHOULDN'T be at zero.  You can't judge whether there is a
shoulder to the detection function by looking at the frequencies of
detections (unlike for line transect sampling).  That is why Distance
produces two plots for each analysis - one corresponding to frequencies
of detections (the 'probability density function'), and the other of
scaled frequencies, with the fitted detection function.  The latter plot
allows you to assess whether there is a shoulder.

Steve Buckland

messages.body_plain:
Dear Colin and others,
we are presently working along the same lines. A student of mine is
programming a model where you can import your real GIS landscape, ideal
transects, and real transects. The idea is to put in various known
population that have:
- variable amounts of clumping (e.g. from random to very clmped)
- and a range of cluster sizes that equals the observed ditsribution

Additionally, there will also be the possibility to vary the probability of
detection based on the distance to the transect and to allow movement of the
animals during the survey. The output of each simulation will look like the
output of a real survey.

My original idea was to feed this simulated data back into program DISTANCE.
However, the program is obviously not made to process 1000 repications :)
So I would appreshiate any help with implementing the math behind DISTANCE
into the simulation model.

The aim is to have a model running and analysis for our study area in
Mongolia within the next 6-9 months. The model could be a nice tool to help
with field design in other areas as well.

I would appreshiate an comments or advise on our modelling approach.
Thanks,
Petra Kaczensky

messages.subject: Re: Distance script
messages.body_plain:
Hi Petra, Colin, list:

First: We (Distance development team) would like to implement spatially
explicit simulations of distance sampling surveys on animal populations
in the Distance software, and indeed have a grant proposal submitted at
present that would provide funding to do this.  Distance can already
work with GIS data, and can already simulate surveys based on input
design criteria.  What is needed is an interface and engine to generate
animal populations and something to simulate the process of observing
the animals given the transect lines.  If you already have a competent
programmer working on this, then we'd be very happy to collaborate and
perhaps you could get something that can work within Distance.  Perhaps
we can discuss this off the list.

Second: The WiSP library for R is already capable of simulating animal
populations (in quite complex spatial configurations) and distance
sampling (as well as other types of) surveys on these populations.  The
limitation is that it can only cope with rather simple study areas
(rectangles) and survey designs.  For more info, see
http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/estimating.abundance/WiSP/index.html

Third: The analysis engines in Distance *are* set up to process 1000
replications or more.  You can call them easily from outside of the
Distance interface.  The CDS/MCDS engine is a FORTRAN program, and the
new MRDS engine is an R library.  An example of calling the MCDS engine
from outside of the Distance interface is given by Eric Rexstad in the
following tech report
http://eprints.st-andrews.ac.uk/archive/00000447/
I have also previously posted on this list about various other options,
and there is something about this in the Distance online manual (MCDS
appendix).  There is a small Visual Basic 6 project on the Support page
of the Distance web pages that demonstrates calling the Distance 4
version of the CDS engine from VB.  I can update this to Distance 5 if
that would be useful.  Bottom line is: I would not recommend
re-implementing the analysis capabilities of Distance in some other
software as part of your simulations -- instead, call what's there!

Hope some of this is some use.  Cheers,

  - Len Thomas

messages.subject: Re: standar error formula
messages.body_plain:
Alejandro-

Standard error is a measure of precision for a parameter estimate(estimator)
Standard deviation is a measure of variation of the data around a mean

This can become confusing because texts will use the term standard
deviation of the mean which is really a standard error for the mean.  If
s is the standard deviation of the data for n measurements, then  the
standard error of the mean is s divided by the square root of n.  This
relationship between the standard deviation of the data and the standard
error only holds for an estimated mean. An estimated mean is an estimate
of a parameter (population mean).

The formulas for the standard errors of parameters (square root of the
parameter variance) in distance sampling are given in the Distance
Sampling book. The outputted standard errors do NOT need to be divided
by sqrt(n) if that was the reason for your question.

regards --jeff
